title: Upset
text:
Upset plots are a visualisation method to display intersections between sets. They can be seen as a different form of a venn diagram but are able to effectively display many intersecting sets.
In this section we will:

title: Upset
text:
Intersecting sets



Intersection plots for community analysis can be used to display the number of intersecting features (e.g. taxa) between samples or sample groups. In other words you can display the shared presence of features between groups.
Additionally, you can flip it around to display the number of intersecting groups between taxa. This allows you to determine which taxa are common and uncommon across the groups. We will see this later on.

title: Upset
text:
Venn versus Upset
Venn diagrams and upset plots display the intersections between sets. To demonstrate the concept of intersecting sets this section includes a few examples of these plots. These plots will display:

Sets of samples (e.g. S1, S2, & S3)
The intersection of phyla


3 way venn diagram
Three way venn digrams are a classic for visualising intersecting sets. Below is an example showing the number of intersecting phyla across three sets of samples (S1, S2, & S3).



 This above plot shows:

6 phyla are found in all samples.
3 phyla are present in S1 and S3 but not S2.
1 phylum is found in S2 that are not present in S1 or S3.
There are a total of 25 phyla (4+2+1+3+6+3+6=10)


MCQs



Please attempt the below MCQs based on the above venn diagram.

How many phyla are present in S2 & S3 but not S1?

 3 18 6



How many phyla are present in S3 but not S1 or S2?

 3 18 6



How many total phyla are present in S3?

 3 18 6





4 way venn digram
Although venn diagrams can be nice, they become more difficult to parse as more sets are included. Below is a 4 way venn diagram to demonstrate this. It includes the same samples as the above venn diagram but with S4 added in.





Upset plot
Instead of venn diagrams we can use upset plots. Below is an upset plots made from the same data as the above 4 way venn diagram. It consists of 2 parts:

A bar chart of the number of phyla found in the intersections of samples.
The intersections of samples displayed with dots and lines.

By default the order of the x-axis is ordered from frequency within the intersections. I.e. from intersection with highest phyla count to lowest phyla count.



 The first three bars/columns of the above plot shows:

S3 has 5 unique phyla.
There are 4 phyla found in all the samples.
S1 & S4 share three phyla not present in S2 or S3.

On important note is that intersections with values of 0 are not displayed in upset plots.

MCQs



Please attempt the below MCQs based on the above upset plot.

How many phyla are present in S1, S3, and S2 but not S4?

 12 0 2



How many phyla are only present in S4?

 12 0 2



How many total phyla are present in S2?

 12 0 2

title: Metadata and taxa tibble
text:
Now we’ll create a total abundance tibble of our metadata categories (rows) against the genera (columns).





The first step is to extract our metadata as a tibble with microbiome::sample_tibble().

#Metadata tibble
metadata_tibble <- microbiome::sample_tibble(pseq)
head(metadata_tibble)






  


We will bind our metadata and taxa abundance tables but first lets ensure they have the same order of samples.

#Ensure metadata and otu tibble have same order of samples
metadata_tibble$SampleID == genus_tibble$Sample

All the values are TRUE so the order is the same allowing us to bind the tibbles with dplyr::bind_cols.

#bind metadata and genus tibbles
genus_metadata_tibble <- dplyr::bind_cols(metadata_tibble, genus_tibble)
head(genus_metadata_tibble)






  


Finally to tidy up the tibble we will remove all the non taxa columns except for the “site” column. We are going to use the sites as the sets for our upset plot.
Carry this out with dplyr::select()

#Create tibble with site and taxa columns
#Create vector of "site" and the genus names
#The -1 is to remove the "Sample" column name
cols_to_keep <- c("site", colnames(genus_tibble[,-1]))
#Subset tibble to our desired columns
site_genus_tibble <- genus_metadata_tibble |>
    #Select all of the columns specified in vector cols_to_keep
    select(all_of(cols_to_keep))

title: Sample and taxa tibble
text:
The first step is to extract the genus abundance table and then transpose it.
Transposing is vital for the next step as it means that:

Each column is a taxa (except the Sample column)
Each row is a sample






Carry out aggregation and transposing.

#Abundance tibble of samples (rows) against genera (columns)
genus_tibble  <- pseq |>
    #Aggregate to genus
    microbiome::aggregate_taxa("Genus", verbose = FALSE) |>
    #Extract otu_table
    phyloseq::otu_table() |>
    #Convert to data.frame and transpose
    as.data.frame() |> t() |>
    #Convert to tibble
    dplyr::as_tibble(rownames = "Sample")
#Display top 6 rows of tibble
head(genus_tibble)




You may notice that we do not use the function microbiome::otu_tibble() in the above code. This is because transposing a tibble will convert our tibble into a transposed matrix rather than a transposed tibble. This matrix has our column names in the first row which we do not want. Therefore, it is easier to go from phyloseq -> otu_table -> data.frame -> transposed -> tibble. Annoyingly complex but
If you want to see this in action you can type and run the below demonstrative code.

#Demonstration on why we don't use microibome::otu_tibble()
pseq |>
    #Aggregate to genus
    microbiome::aggregate_taxa("Genus", verbose = FALSE) |>
    #Extract otu_table as a tibble
    microbiome::otu_tibble() |>
    #Transpose
    t() |>
    #View top 6 rows
    head()

title: Sample and taxa tibble
Sample and taxa tibble
All in one code
text:
All in one code



We’ll create another upset plot with two main differences.

It will display the intersection of the phyla sets against sample grouping.
We’ll create and run one pipeline that goes from the ASV abundance phyloseq object to an upset plot.

Read through, type, and run the code. Ensure you understand how it all works before continuing.
Please feel free to copy, paste, and edit previous code to create the below code. This code will then be useful for copy, pasting, and editing to create further plots.

#Upset plot of phyla intersections with sample groupings
phyla_samples_upset_plot <- pseq |>
    #Convert abundances to relative/compositional abundances
    microbiome::transform("compositional") |>
    #Aggregate ASVs to phylum level
    microbiome::aggregate_taxa("Phylum", verbose = FALSE) |>
    #Extract phyla relative abundance table
    phyloseq::otu_table() |>
    #Extract otu_table as a tibble
    microbiome::otu_tibble(column.id = "Phylum") |>
    #Longify tibble
    tidyr::pivot_longer(!Phylum, names_to="Sample", values_to="Abundance") |>
    #Filter out rows were relative abundance is 0
    #i.e. retain rows showing presence
    dplyr::filter(Abundance > 0) |>
    #Select to remove unwanted Abundance column
    dplyr::select(-Abundance) |>
    #Group tibble by the Sample (grouping) column
    dplyr::group_by(Sample) |>
    #Summarise the Phylum (sets) column
    #Results in each row having a unique sample
    # with a list of the intersection of present phyla
    dplyr::summarize(Phyla = list(Phylum)) |>
    #ggplot
    #Phyla (intersection) column as the x aesthetic
    ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = Phyla)) +
        #Bar chart
        ggplot2::geom_bar() +
        #Upset scale on x axis
        ggupset::scale_x_upset() + 
        #Y label
        ggplot2::labs(y="Sample count")

title: Rare removal
text:
In this page we will quickly discuss and show how to use lower taxa levels with rare removal. This involves:

Determining the number of different taxa at a certain level.
Removing rare features (taxa) through rare aggregation.
Formatting the data and producing an upset plot.

This upset plot will display the intersection of genera (sets) against the samples (groups).
We remove rare features for a few reasons:

To many sets will make it hard to make a clear plot.
Rare features (taxa) will most likely only add noise when looking at the prominent features (taxa).






The easiest method to determine the number of taxa groups at a certain taxonomic level is by aggregating the phyloseq object and display the dimension data of the objects within the aggregated phyloseq object.
Carry this out for Genus level.

#Aggregate taxa to genus
#This will also display the dimensions of the tables and data within the phyloseq object
microbiome::aggregate_taxa(pseq, level = "Genus")

This shows we have 172 taxa (i.e. 172 unique genera). This would be to much to visualise in an upset plot so lets reduce that number by removing rare genera (i.e. genera with low abundances across the data).






To remove the rare genera we will aggregate the taxa whilst carrying out rare aggregation. This combines rare genera into one taxa group called “Other”. We will then remove this “Other” group as it won’t be interesting to include in our upset plot.
For more information on rare aggregation please see our R community analysis workbook.
Carry out rare aggregation and removal.

#Aggregate to genus and remove rare genera
genus_rareaggregate_pseq <- pseq |>
    #Convert to compositional values
    microbiome:::transform("compositional") |>
    #Use thresholds of at least 0.5% relative abundance (detection)
    # in at least 10% of samples (prevalence)
    #Thresholds chosen as they lead to a manageable amount of taxa
    microbiome::aggregate_rare(level = "Genus",
                                detection = 0.005, prevalence = 1/10) |>
    #Remove the "Other" genus which consists of all the rare aggregated taxa
    phyloseq::subset_taxa(Genus != "Other")
#Overview of phyloseq object
genus_rareaggregate_pseq

This lead to a phyloseq object with 29 taxa which seems like a good number of sets to create an upset plot with.






With our rare removed genus phyloseq object we can create an upset plot with:

Intersection of genera sets.
Samples as the groups.


#Upset plot code
genus_rare_removed_samples_upset_plot <- genus_rareaggregate_pseq |>
    #Extract otu_table as a tibble
    microbiome::otu_tibble(column.id = "Genus") |>
    #Longify tibble
    tidyr::pivot_longer(!Genus, names_to="Sample", values_to="Abundance") |>
    #Filter out rows were relative abundance is 0
    #i.e. retain rows showing presence
    dplyr::filter(Abundance > 0) |>
    #Select to remove unwanted Abundance column
    dplyr::select(-Abundance) |>
    #Group tibble by the Sample (grouping) column
    dplyr::group_by(Sample) |>
    #Summarise the Genus (sets) column
    #Results in each row having a unique sample (group)
    # with a list of the intersection of present genera
    dplyr::summarize(Genera = list(Genus)) |>
    #ggplot
    #Genera (intersection) column as the x aesthetic
    ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = Genera)) +
        #Bar chart
        ggplot2::geom_bar() +
        #Upset scale on x axis
        ggupset::scale_x_upset() + 
        #Y label
        ggplot2::labs(y="Sample count")
#Save plot to png file
ggplot2::ggsave(filename = "./genus_rare_removed_intersection_sample_group_upset.png", 
                plot = genus_rare_removed_samples_upset_plot,
                device = "png", dpi = 300, units = "mm", height = 200, width = 300)
#Dsplay plot in jupyter notebook
IRdisplay::display_png(file="./genus_rare_removed_intersection_sample_group_upset.png")

Great, you know how to create an upset plot based on a specific taxa level with rare taxa removed. What if you want to see the intersection of rare features?

title: Random effects
text:
A random effect is a categorical control variable to include that you are not necessarily interested in evaluating but you want to control for. These include:

Experimental blocks
Common spatial groupings that create non-independence (e.g. samples from the same people or country)
Temporal groupings that also create non-independence (e.g. samples collected from different places in the same year)

In our analysis we are using the Plate variable as a random effect.


Random effects are always included by writing elements in () with a |. On the left of the | you specify the random effect/s. On the right of the | you specify the grouping factor/s on which the random effects depend on, these must be categorical.
Examples include:

(1|s): Random intercepts for unique level of factor s
(1|s) + (1|i): Random intercept for each unique level of s and each unique level of i
(1|s/i): Random intercepts for factor s and i, where the random effects of i are nested in s

Expands to (1|s) + (1|s:i), i.e. a random intercept for each level of s, and each unique combination of the levels s and i
Nested random effects are used in so-called multilevel models
For example, s might refer to schools/forest, and i to classroom/tree within the school/forest

(a|s): Random intercept and random slopes for a, for each level of s

Correlations between the intercept and slope effects are also estimated

(a*b|s): Random intercepts and slopes for a, b, and the a:b interaction, for each level of s.

Correlation between all the random effects are estimated

(0+a|s): Random slopes for a for each level of s, but no random intercepts
(a||s): Random intercepts and random slopes for a, for each level of s, but no correlations between the random effect (i.e. they are set to 0)

Expands to (0+a|s) + (1|s)


You are most likely to only use grouping factors ((1|grouping_effect)). In our formula our random effect specification is (1|Plate) so we are using Plate as a grouping effect.








Random effects may not be suitable when there are fewer than 4 average observations per random effect group. Small random effect groups may produce poor model fits from logistic/prevalence random intercept models. Generally small random effects do not cause an issue for linear/abundance models.
Recommendations:

>= 4 average observations per group

e.g. subject sampled >= 4 times
Use subject as random effect
Set small_random_effects=FALSE (default)
Random effects are robust and increase power

< 4 average observations per group, metadata not collinear with the groups

e.g. Subjects sampled once before and once after treatment
Use subject as random effect
Set small_random_effect=TRUE

Abundance testing will use random effects as random effects
Prevalence testing will use random effects as fixed effects

Prevalence random effects are not robust but fixed effects are robust and control for grouping

< 4 average observations per group, metadata collinear with the groups

e.g. Subjects have fixed disease status and are sampled twice

Each subject has the same disease status for all their data points, therefore subject and disease status are collinear

Subset or average data to one observation per group (i.e. have one observation per subject)
Reminder: This only benefits prevalence testing as abundance testing is not greatly affected by small random effects


Therefore, it is always good to check the number of observations per group of your random effects. The below code uses the functions dplyr::count() to show this for our Plate variable as an example.

#Number of observations for each plate
metadf |>
    dplyr::count(Plate)

In this case all our observations have >=4 so our average will also be >= 4. Using small_random_effects=FALSE in our maaslin3() analysis would be the correct choice. You should check this before running maaslin3() in your own analysis when using random effects.
It is not always easy to determine whether the average is >=4 by viewing them all. You can quickly calculate the average with the below code.

#Average number of observations per group
metadf |>
    dplyr::count(Plate) |>
    dplyr::pull(n) |> mean()

title: Categorical linear boxplots
text:
Boxplots are used to visualise relative/linear modelling associations with categorical fixed effects. To learn about these we will look at the Soil association to interpret the metrics and plots. As a reminder we used Bulk Soil as the reference and Rhizosphere Soil as the query.
In this page we will:

Create a significant results table with only abundance model and Soil rows
Explain the coefficient value
View and display box plots








To start we’ll create a significant result tibble only containing Soil associations with the abundance model.

#Tibble of significant abundance associations for Soil
sig_res_soil_abund_tbl <- sig_res_tbl |> 
    #Filter to retain metadata Soil rows
    dplyr::filter(metadata == "Soil") |>
    #Filter to retain abundance model rows
    dplyr::filter(model == "abundance")
#Glimpse the tibble
sig_res_soil_abund_tbl |> dplyr::glimpse()

With this tibble we’ll extract the top 5 associations by their q-values (qval_individual).

#Top 5 lowest qval individual values species by abundance for Soil
sig_res_soil_abund_tbl |> 
    #Extract the five rows with the smallest qval_individual values
    dplyr::slice_min(qval_individual, n=5) |>

title: Continuous logistic boxplots
text:
Box plots are used to visualise prevalence/logistic modelling associations with continuous effects. These show the range of read sizes for samples where the feature is absent and samples where the feature is absent.
We will use the Reads grouping to look at continuous logistic results.
In this page we will:

Create a significant results table with only prevalence model and read rows
Explain the coefficient value
View and display box plots








Create a significant result tibble only containing Reads associations with the prevalence model.

#Create a tbl with our sig results of interest
sig_res_reads_prev_tbl <- sig_res_tbl |> 
    #Filter to retain metadata Reads rows
    dplyr::filter(metadata == "Reads") |>
    #Filter to retain prevalence model rows
    dplyr::filter(model == "prevalence")
#Glimpse the tibble
sig_res_reads_prev_tbl |> dplyr::glimpse()

Extract the top 5 associations by their q-values (qval_individual).

#Top 5 significant associations for prevalence modelling of Reads
sig_res_reads_prev_tbl |>
    #Extract the five rows with the smallest qval_individual values
    dplyr::slice_min(qval_individual, n=5) |>
    #Select rows of interest
    dplyr::select(c(1:5,9,12,14,15))









Let’s look at the top association:

Feature: Azospira
Coefficient: 2.360408
Q-value: 0.012062

For continuous metadata the coefficient represents the amount of increased/decreased likelihood of the feature’s presence with a higher value of the metadata. A positive value for Reads would indicate the feature is more likely to be present with samples of higher read counts. In other words a positive coefficient means the logit of the feature being present increases.








Logistic continuous plots are horizontal box plots of read counts separated into 2 groupings:

Samples where the feature is absent
Samples where the feature is present

Let’s look at an example.


Below is the box plot created for the logistic modelling of Pilimelia for the reads effect.





In this case the plot shows:

Samples where the feature are present tend to have higher read counts
There are more samples where the feature is absent (N (not zero) = 16) compared to where it is absent (64-16=48).










View the associations with negative coefficients in sig_res_reads_prev_tbl.

#Significant associations with negative coefficients
# for prevalence modelling of Reads
sig_res_reads_prev_tbl |>
    #Retain rows with a coefficient value less than 0
    dplyr::filter(coef < 0) |>
    #Select rows of interest
    dplyr::select(c(1:5,9,11,12,14,15)) |>
    #Arrange by individual q-value
    dplyr::arrange(qval_individual)

From this we can see that we have 12 associations. This is in contrast to the 129 positive associations (141-12=129). However, there are some caveats to these negative associations.
Only four of the associations do not have errors. The other eight have the error: “Prevalence association possibly induced by stronger abundance association”.
The most important feature to notice is that only 4 of the associations are significant (qval_individual<0.1). The other eight are included because their joint q-values are < 0.1.
It makes sense that you are more likely to get positive coefficient values for reads. The more reads you have the more likely you are to detect all organisms present.

title: Significant results table
text:
There are various output files in our output directory genus_output. The first we will look at is the text file significant_results.tsv. This contains all the significant features maaslin3() found.
This significance is based on the individual q-value or the joint q-value. Additionally, the rows are ordered from most to least significant (i.e. ascending order based on the qval_individual column).







Save then close and halt your “2-MaAsLin3.ipynb” notebook.
Create and open a new jupyter notebook called “3-Text_output.ipynb”.
Create a markdown cell at the top with:

# 3-Text output
## Libraries

In a code cell load the required libraries.

#Library
library("DT")
library("tidyverse")









To view the significant results we need to first read in the file. In this case we’ll read it in as a tibble with readr::read_delim() and then glimpse it.

sig_res_tbl <- readr::read_delim(
    file="./genus_output/significant_results.tsv",
    delim="\t")
sig_res_tbl |> dplyr::glimpse()

There are many columns/variables which are explained in the next page: Metrics.








To load the significant results easily in other notebooks we’ll save the sig_res_tbl object as a file.

#Save significant reults tibble
save(sig_res_tbl, file="./genus_output/significant_results.RData")









You can view the whole table in R:

sig_res_tbl

With this object you can carry out various commands to pull out specific data.
Optionally, you can open the file (significant_results.tsv) by navigating to the genus_output directory through your jupyter file explorer. Once in the directory you can click on the file to open it.
Neither of these methods are convenient. In your own future analysis you can use excel but we’ll show you another option below.








We can create a html table with the package DT and its function DT::datatable(). In the function we specify the data.frame/tibble to convert to HTML. Additionally, we specify options = list(pageLength = 20) so the resulting html will show 20 rows at a time.
DT package homepage

#Convert table to html
sig_res_dt <- DT::datatable(sig_res_tbl, options = list(pageLength = 20))

The above code created an R object which we then need to save as an HTML file. We’ll carry this out with htmlwidgets::saveWidget(). The option selfcontained = must be set to TRUE for this to function correctly.
htmlwidgets::savewdigets() code documentation

#Save HTML
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(
    #Input widget/html
    widget = sig_res_dt,
    #Output html
    file = "./genus_output/significant_results.html",
    #Save as a single self contained HTML
    selfcontained = TRUE)









With the HTML created navigate into the genus_output directory via the jupyter file browser. Click on your HTML file (significant_results.html) to open it.
The html is interactive with the following features:

Order the table by a specific column by clicking on its column name

Click on it once for descending order
Click on it twice for ascending order

Set the number of rows to display with the drop down on the top left (“Show X entries”)

Choices are: 10, 20, 25, 50, and 100

Search for specific text/numbers with the search bar on the top right

Useful if you are interested in the results of a specific species or genus

Navigate across the pages with the arrows and page numbers on the bottom right
View the total number of rows (i.e. significant features) on the bottom left

title: Metadata
text:
As with most analysis we require metadata. Our metadata table requires:

Columns of the different metadata variables

The column names are the names of the variables

Rows of observations per sample

The row names need to contain the same sample names as the count table









Extract and check our metadata.

#Extract metadata from phyloseq as a data.frame
metadf <- genus_pseq |> 
    microbiome::meta()
#Check rows 1:5
metadf |> dplyr::slice(1:5)







TipTidyverse functions used above




dplyr::slice()











There are three main types of metadata variables for MaAsLin3. These are:

Categorical fixed effects

A categorical variable that is related to your hypothesis and requires evaluation
These need to be factors in your metadata

The first level is the reference group
All other levels are compared to the reference in pairwise fashion (i.e. the query)
For example healthy vs disease states

We will use Soil as a categorical fixed effect (you can have more than one)

Continuous fixed effects

This could be a continuous variable that is related to your hypothesis and requires evaluation (e.g. dosage)
Or it could be a continuous control variable (e.g. age)
We will use Reads (read counts/depth) as a continuous control variable (see the read counts page)

Random effects

Categorical variables to include that you are not necessarily interested in evaluating
These don’t need to be factors since a reference group is not required
An example includes experimental blocks, different sequencing runs, or subjects
We will use Plate (plate used for sequencing) as a random effect


More theory and considerations are included in the later pages:

Fixed effects
Random effects









We are going to use Soil as a categorical fixed effect. Therefore, we need to set the order of its factor levels.






NoteFactors





A factor is R’s way of storing categorical data. It tells the model to compare categories, and lets us set which category is used as the reference level.
For more info please see: R primer for omics explanation of factors



Before factor ordering, let’s see what groupings are in the Soil variable.

#Check unique values of Soil
metadf |> dplyr::pull(Soil) |> unique()







TipTidyverse functions used above




dplyr::pull()



We have 2 for Soil. Let’s use Bulk Soil as the reference group and Rhizosphere Soil as the query.
Type and run the below code to order the factor levels of the two metadata variables. The code uses some piping and the dplyr::mutate() function.

#Factorise to order our categorical fixed effects
metadf <- metadf |>
    #Factorise Soil with Bulk Soil as the reference level
    dplyr::mutate(Soil=factor(Soil,
                              levels = c("Bulk Soil","Rhizosphere Soil")))







TipTidyverse functions used above




dplyr::mutate()









Note



For the purposes of setting a reference it only matters which group is set as the first group. If you have more than one query group their level order does not matter for the MaAsLin3 analysis we will carry out.


Great! Next we’ll add read counts/depth to the metadata table.

title: Fixed effects
text:
Fixed effects are any term related to your hypothesis that requires evaluation and any continuous control variables.
We are interested in the differences between our two soil types sites (Bulk Soil and Rhizosphere Soil) so we used it as a fixed effect.
To control for the read counts/depths of the samples we used Reads as a fixed effect. This uses it as a continuous control variable.


When using fixed effects you can look at the main effect, interactions, or both of multiple variables.
The main effects is when looking at the effect of one variable by itself. Interactions are used to test whether the effect of one predictor variable on the outcome changes depending on another predictor variable. For example, an interaction between treatment and time point tests whether the treatment effect is different at different time points.
In our formula we specified the formula to only look at main effects.



Below is a list of examples on how to specify the usage of fixed effects.

a: Main effect of a
a + b: Main effect of a and b (no interaction)
a:b: Interaction of a and b (no main effects)
a * b: Main effects and interaction of a and b (expands to a + b + a:b)
(a+b+c)^2: Main effects and 2-way interactions (no 3-way interaction) of a, b , and c (expands to a + b + c + a:b + a:c + b:c)
(a+b)*c: all main effects and pairwise interactions between a and c, and b and c (not between a and b) (expands to a + b + c + a:c + b:c)
0 + a: 0 suppresses the intercept resulting in a model that has one parameter per level of a (identical to : a - 1)







Tip



The maaslin3() developers recommend combining 2 fixed effect columns into one for interactions rather than the a:b method. For example, with our Durance river dataset you could combine the Site and Media columns into one called site.media and use it as a main effect to see the interactions of Site and Media rather than using Site:Media in the formula.

title: Plot types
text:
As a recap the four different types of plots are below.


For abundance associations.


Box plot showing the log base 2 relative abundance values of the features.





Coefficient represents the fold change from the reference to the query group.



Scatter plot of log base 2 relative abundance (y) against continuous effect (x, read depth in below figure) with best fit line.





Coefficient represents the amount of change the variable causes, i.e. the slope.




For prevalence associations.


Tile plot showing the number of samples where the feature is present and absent for each grouping.





The coefficient indicates the difference of log-odds/logit of the feature being present in query samples compared to the reference samples.



Box plot of the continuous value (read depth in below figure) split by samples where the feature is present and absent.





The coefficient represents the amount of increased/decreased likelihood (log-odds/logit) of the feature’s presence with a higher value of the metadata.

title: MaAsLin3
text:
MaAsLin3 is a tool to detect feature associations based on metadata groupings using mixed effect models.
It carries out 2 types of association tests:

Abundance testing

Determines the difference in the abundance values between groups
Carried out with linear modelling

Prevalence testing

Determines the likelihood of features being present based on groupings
Carried out with logistic modelling


Both tests produce q-values plus a joint q-value is given.

Linear regression: Theory of linear models for abundance testing

title: Genus aggregation
text:
All taxa levels from phyla to species to ASVs can be used with MaAsLin3. In fact, in your own research I would recommend carrying out MaAsLin3 analysis on multiple taxa levels.
For speed and to produce clear results we will carry out MaAsLin3 analysis with genus counts.







Use the function microbiome::aggregate_taxa() to produce a genus count based phyloseq object.

#Aggregate ASV based phyloseq to genus phyloseq
genus_pseq <- microbiome::aggregate_taxa(pseq, "Genus", verbose=FALSE)







Note



Biomarker detection/differential abundance allows you to determine if rare taxa are differentially abundant. Due to this I would not reccomend aggregating rare taxa with microbiome::aggregate_rare() unless you have a good reason.


Check the phyloseq object and number of genera.

#Summarise
microbiome::summarize_phyloseq(genus_pseq)
#Number of genera
nrow(phyloseq::otu_table(genus_pseq))




We won’t need the ASV phyloseq object anymore so you can remove it.

#Remove pseq object
rm(pseq)

title: Count table
text:
The count table for MaAsLin3 needs to be a data.frame with:

Columns names of features

In our case genera

Row names of sample names
Values of counts

In our case abundance values








Note



As it requires row names the count table cannot be a tibble.









Extract the otu_table (i.e. count table) from the genus phyloseq object as a matrix.

#Extract otu_table as matrix
taxa_df <- genus_pseq |>
    microbiome::abundances()
#Check
taxa_df[1:5,1:10]









Our count table is currently not in the correct format so we will need to use some base R and dplyr() functions to manipulate it. This includes:

title: Metrics
text:
There are various metrics in the output text files of maaslin3(). Each row is a single association based on a combination of a single feature, the specific metadata comparison, and the model used (abundance or prevalence).







There is a lot of information in this file as can be seen in the number of metrics below.
Although the metrics are important they do not give a full picture of the results. Rather it is better to use the metrics and plots together.








Both the files all_results.tsv and significant_results.tsv have the following columns/metrics:

feature: Feature name

Features are species in our data

metadata: Metadata name (e.g. Soil or Reads)
value: Metadata value

Categorical: The query group name (e.g. Rhizosphere Soil)
Continuous: The metadata name (e.g. Reads)

name: Variable name from model

Categorical: The metadata name and query group name combined (e.g. SoilRhizosphere Soil)
Continuous: The metadata name (e.g. Reads)

coef: The fit coefficient

Abundance models: A one-unit change in metadata variable corresponds to 2coef fold change in the relative abundance of the feature
Prevalence models: A one-unit change in the metadatum variable corresponds to a coef change in the log-odds/logit of a feature being present
This is covered more in the output plot section

null_hypothesis: The value of the null hypothesis against which the coefficient is tested

This value is zero when median comparison is off
This value is the median value when median comparison is on, see median comparison
In our results abundance model rows are median and prevalence model rows are 0

pval_individual: The p-value of the individual association
qval_individual: The false discovery rate (FDR) corrected q-value of the individual association

FDR correction is performed over all p-values without errors in the abundance and prevalence modelling together

pval_joint: p-value of the joint prevalence and abundance association

More info below
Calculated from plugging in the minimum of the association’s abundance and prevalence p-values into the Beta(1,2) CDF
Interpreted as the probability that either the abundance or prevalence association would be as extreme as observed if there was neither an abundance nor prevalence association between the feature and metadatum

qval_joint: q-value of the joint prevalence and abundance association
error: Lists any errors from the model fitting
model: Specifies whether the association is abundance or prevalence
N: Total number of data points for the feature
N_not_zero: Total number of non-zero data points for the feature

i.e. number of samples where the feature is present










The Individual p-value is the p-value from the linear/abundance or logistic/prevalence model testing depending on the value of the model column. It’s q-value indicates if the association is significant (<0.1) or not (>=0.1).
The joint p-value is equal to pbeta(min_p_value,1,2), where:

pbeta(): Function to generate probability density values for the Beta Distribution

Function webpage

min_p_value: The minimum value between the abundance and prevalence modelling p-values of the feature comparison
1,2: In essence represents 1 out of 2







Note



There is an exception to this calculation. If one of the 2 associations has an error or an NA for its p-value then the joint p-value is the p-value of the other association.


In essence this is a form of multiple test testing due to the fact we are running 2 tests for each feature comparison (abundance and prevalence).
It can be useful in the below situations:

The abundance test of a comparison is significant but the prevalence test is insignificant

If the joint p-value is insignificant then it is likely the abundance p-value may not be as extreme, i.e. its significant p-value came about by chance

The prevalence test of a comparison is significant but the abundance test is insignificant

If the joint p-value is insignificant then it is likely the prevalence p-value may not be as extreme, i.e. its significant p-value came about by chance


Generally this is only a concern if the significant p-value is very near significance (i.e. a bit lower than 0.1). If this is the case and the joint p-value is not significant (>=0.1) we should be sceptical of the association.
If both the individual p/q-values of the association (abundance & prevalence) are significant we can generally ignore the joint p/q-value.
For this and your future analysis we recommend using the q-values rather than p-values.

title: MaAsLin3 function
text:
For our analysis we will immediately run the maaslin3() function.
Additionally, this section contains a lot of theory on the following:

lme4 specification: The formula containing the fixed and random effects
Fixed effects: The effects your hypothesis are interested in
Random effects: Effects your hypothesis may not necessarily be interested in but you want to control for
Median comparison: When to and when not to use median comparison in association testing








Create and open a new jupyter notebook called “2-MaAsLin3.ipynb”.
Create a markdown cell at the top with:

# 2-MaAsLin3
## Libraries

In a code cell load the required libraries and data.

#Libraries
library("maaslin3")
library("tidyverse")
#Load data
load("genus_taxa_df.RData")
load("metadf.RData")

Check the top of our metadata to see the variable names to be used for masslin3() below.








Run the MaAsLin3 analysis.

#Set a random seed
set.seed(419)
#MaAsLin3
fit_out <- maaslin3(input_data=taxa_df,
                    input_metadata=metadf,
                    output='genus_output',
                    formula='~ Soil + Reads + (1|Plate)',
                    normalization='TSS',
                    transform='LOG',
                    augment=TRUE,
                    standardize=TRUE,
                    max_significance=0.1,
                    median_comparison_abundance=TRUE,
                    median_comparison_prevalence=FALSE,
                    small_random_effects=FALSE,
                    max_pngs=250,
                    cores=1)
#Set random seed back to null
set.seed(NULL)







Important



The above command will take a while. As it runs please read the below and other pages in this section.










The parameters we have used are described below.

input_data: Our formatted count table containing abundance values of species against samples
input_metadata: Our formatted metadata table for our samples
output: Name of output directory

This will be created by the function

formula: The comparison formula in lme4 specification

Details in lme4 formula page

normalization: Normalisation of the counts before transformation and analysis. Options include:

'TTS' (default): Total Sum Scaling

Converts the counts to fractional relative abundance values so total count of each sample = 1

'CLR': Centred Log Ratio
'NONE': No normalisation

transform: Transformation of feature counts after normalisation but before analysis

Allows MaAsLin3 and us to see the log difference of features between comparisons/groups
Options include:

LOG: Base 2 log transformation (recommended)

Our TSS normalised values will all become -ve values or 0 (log(1, base=2) = 0, log(0.1, base=2)=-3.321928)

PLOG: Pseudo-log with a pseudo-count of half the dataset’s minimum non-zero abundance replacing zeroes

Suggested for metabolomics data

NONE


augment: Default is TRUE

Avoids linear separability and is almost always recommended

standardise: When TRUE it applies z-scores to continuous metadata variables so they are on the same scale

The default is TRUE and is recommended
Allows comparison of coefficients across metadata variables

max_significance: FDR corrected q-value threshold for significance

This will determine what associations are written as signifiant and what plots are created
Associations with an individual or joint q-value less than the threshold will be included in the significant results out
Only associations with an individual q-value lower than the threshold will be plotted

median_comparison_abundance & median_comparison_prevalence: Whether to compare coefficients against median coefficient (TRUE) or against 0 (FALSE)

For normal taxa abundance data set median_comparison_abundance = TRUE and median_comparison_prevalence = FALSE
More info, including when to use TRUE and FALSE, in Median comparison page

small_random_effect: Replace random effects with fixed effects in logistic prevalence model

default FALSE
Use TRUE to handle low number of observations per group
More information in the Random effect page


Full information here: MaAslin3 analysis options

title: Read counts
text:
MaAsLin3 can test whether metadata variables are associated with feature presence/absence. This is called a prevalence test.
Prevalence of organisms can be greatly affected by the read depth of the different samples. When using abundance values (not quantitative abundance values) the read numbers/depth for each sample should be included as a continuous fixed effect.






NoteQuantitative abundance?





Quantitative abundances (aka absolute abundances) are the actual count of cells in an environment. With the correct protocol this can be calculated, such as through qPCR and 16S rRNA spike-ins. This approach is still relatively rare.
Some people like to call non-quantitative abundances as relative abundance values (i.e. normal 16S rRNA approach). However I find this confusing. Instead I like to use the following 3 terms for normal 16S rRNA counts:

Abundance/counts: The 16S counts without any normalisation
Relative abundance: The 16S counts normalised to fractions so each sample has a total count of 1
Rarefied abundances: Normalised 16S counts made of whole numbers (>=1), via subsampling, so each sample has the same total count/depth

More information about absolute abundances and how to analyse them can be found in the official MaAsLin3 manual










We can calculate read depths from our count table with rowSums().

#Calculate read count of each sample
read_counts <- taxa_df |> rowSums()
read_counts

To add these values to our metadata we can create a data.frame containing 2 columns:

Sample: Name of samples matching Sample column in metadf
Reads: The read depth values that we’ll add to metadf


#Convert to data.frame
read_df <- data.frame(names(read_counts), unname(read_counts))
#Change column names
colnames(read_df) <- c("Sample", "Reads")
#Check top of df
read_df |> head()




To add the depths to our metadf data.frame we can use the function dplyr::inner_join(). This function joins 2 data.frames/tibbles ensuring the rows are assigned correctly by a shared column. It is similar to VLOOKUP in excel.
In our case this is the column Sample, ensuring that each sample is assigned the correct read depth value.

#Add read count values to metadf with dplyr::inner_join()
#Similar to excel's vlookup
metadf <- metadf |>
    dplyr::inner_join(read_df, by="Sample")
#Check top of df
metadf |> head()

Unfortunately dplyr::inner_join() removes row names. These are required for our metadf so let’s add them back.

#Add row names back (removed from inner_join)
row.names(metadf) <- metadf$Sample
#Check top of df
metadf |> head()









We’ll open a new jupyter notebook in the next section. Save your taxa_df and metadf objects as files so you can load them into the next notebook.

save(taxa_df,file="genus_taxa_df.RData")
save(metadf,file="metadf.RData")

You can now save then close and halt the notebook.
With our count table and we can move onto the MaAsLin3 analysis.

title: Divergence
text:
Divergence analysis is comparing the dissimilarity distances between (inter-) and within (intra-) groupings. This allows us to more closely examine beta diversity.
Ordination analysis (PCoA, NMDS, etc.) allows us to determine if groups cluster separately by dissimilarity/biodiversity measures. Divergence analysis allows us to determine:

Intra-group divergence/homogeneity: Comparison of distances within a group compared to distances within other groups.
Inter-group divergence/heterogeneity: Comparison of dissimilarity distances between a group’s samples and all other group’s samples (inter-group distances) compared to other groups’ inter-group distances.

To remember the difference between intra- and inter- I remember the intranet (network within an organisation) and the internet (network between organisation). More information about intra- and inter-divergence are in their specific sections.





The sections are:

Setup: Setting up your environment, jupyter-notebook, libraries, and data for the divergence tutorial
Data format: Formatting data for divergence analysis

Involves information about the original dissimilarity matrix and its parts (lower triangle, upper triangle, and diagonal)

Intra-group divergence

Overview of intra-group divergence
Practice with intra-site divergence
Exercise with intra-media divergence

Inter-group divergence

Overview of inter-group divergence
Practice with inter-site divergence
Exercise with inter-media divergence

Advanced/extra

Combining plots into one png
Divergence analysis when splitting by another group (intra-media by intra-site & inter-media by intra-site)

title: Intra-site divergence
text:
For our first intra-group analysis we’ll examine the dissimilarity within the three sites. The sites are different parts of the Durance river:

Upper Durance (UD)
Middle Durance (MD)
Lower Durance (LD)

To analyse the Intra-site divergence we will:

Subset our long tibble of distances and metadata to only contain one set of intra-group distances.
Create a violin plot of the intra-site distances
Carry out a pairwise wilcox test to statistically compare the inter-site divergences between sites.

As a reminder we are using weighted UniFrac distances.





Our first step is to subset our tibble so we only have the intra-site distances.
For this step we pipe (|>) our weighted UniFrac long tibble to 2 different ‘dplyr::filter()’ commands.
First the lower triangle values are kept to remove the upper triangle values. The lower triangle values and upper triangle values are duplicated the difference being which sample is set as the left and right sample. We only want one value from each pair for intra-group divergence as each value will only be used in one divergence grouping.
The next filter step is to only retain samples where the left site grouping (site_L) is the same as the right site grouping (site_R). This means we only retain the intra-site distances. Two important notes:

In you own analyses and the exercise ensure you use the columns for the intra-grouping you are interested in.

E.g. you would use media_L == media_R when analysing intra-media divergence of this dataset.

We removed the intra-sample distances (e.g. sample 1 to sample 1 distance) in our data formatting step as we would never want them for divergence analysis.


#Subset long tibble so only rows where site_L and site_R are identical of the lower triangle
#I.e. the long tibble only contains one set of paired distances within sites (Intra-site) 
intra_site_wunifrac_long_tbl <-
    beta_long_tbl |>
        #Filter to keep lower triangle rows
        dplyr::filter(triangle == "lower") |>
        #Filter to keep rows where site_L is the same as site_R (intra site)
        dplyr::filter(site_L == site_R)
#Check head of long tbl
intra_site_wunifrac_long_tbl |> head()







A box plot is a good method to visualise divergence. However, we’ll make it even nicer by making a violin plot.
In the below plot we separate the values by site using site_L, we could use site_R and their would be no difference as the values in site_L and `site_R are identical.
For a reminder on violin plots please see the R community analysis workbook.

#Intra-site divergence violin plot
intra_site_violin_plot <-

title: Intra-site divergence
text:
Our first step is to subset our tibble so we only have the intra-site distances.
For this step we pipe (|>) our weighted UniFrac long tibble to 2 different ‘dplyr::filter()’ commands.
First the lower triangle values are kept to remove the upper triangle values. The lower triangle values and upper triangle values are duplicated the difference being which sample is set as the left and right sample. We only want one value from each pair for intra-group divergence as each value will only be used in one divergence grouping.
The next filter step is to only retain samples where the left site grouping (site_L) is the same as the right site grouping (site_R). This means we only retain the intra-site distances. Two important notes:

In you own analyses and the exercise ensure you use the columns for the intra-grouping you are interested in.

E.g. you would use media_L == media_R when analysing intra-media divergence of this dataset.

We removed the intra-sample distances (e.g. sample 1 to sample 1 distance) in our data formatting step as we would never want them for divergence analysis.


#Subset long tibble so only rows where site_L and site_R are identical of the lower triangle

    beta_long_tbl |>
        #Filter to keep lower triangle rows
        dplyr::filter(triangle == "lower") |>
        #Filter to keep rows where site_L is the same as site_R (intra site)
        dplyr::filter(site_L == site_R)
#Check head of long tbl
intra_site_wunifrac_long_tbl |> head()

title: Intra-group overview
text:
With our data formatted we will first carry out intra-group divergence analysis. This is analysing the distances within groups (e.g. intranet is a network within an organisation).
In this section we will:

Analyse the Intra-site divergence (River locations: LD, MD, & UD)
Exercise: Repeat the previous steps for Intra-media divergence (CVP, ENV, KBC, & TSA)






When carrying out intra-group divergence we are trying to determine which groups have lower dissimilarity distances between their samples.
If a group has low intra-group distances this indicates the communities of the samples are quite similar. Whereas, if a group has high intra-group distances this indicates the communities of the samples are quite dissimilar.
For example, if you were comparing the gut microbiome of farmed fish compared to wild fish you may find:

Low intra-group distances in the gut microbiome of farmed fish.

This could be caused by their consistent diet and treatment with antibiotics leading to similar gut microbiome profiles.

High intra-group distances in the gut microbiome of wild fish.

This could be due to the variety in their diets and their ability to move through various environments.


You are able to see intra-group divergence of this in ordination plots (PCoA, NMDS etc.) where group clusters being tighter than others indicates lower dissimilarity values. For example the below (fictional) ordination shows tighter clustering in the gut microbiome of farmed fish compared to wild fish.









So why carry out divergence analysis? Divergence analysis directly uses the dissimilarity matrix values rather than ordination values that are calculated from the matrix. Therefore, if you are interested in and making statements about intra-group dissimilarity it is best to carry out visual and statistical intra-group divergence analysis.






With intra-group divergence we look at the dissimilarity distances between all pairs within the same group.


Let’s say we have 3 groups (G1, G2, & G3) each with 3 samples. With this example data we acquire the below ordination plot (e.g. PCoA or NMDS).












In this example data we would have 3 pairs in each group, this can be seen in the below plot. A 4 sample group would have 6 pairs, and a 5 sample group would have 10 pairs. To calculate the number of pairs in a set you can use n(n-1)/2.
The below plot shows a line between each sample and its intra-group pairs. We will only use the distances of these pairs for our intra-group divergence analysis.
Note: We use the beta diversity distance (e.g. UniFrac) not the ordination distance (e.g. PCoA) for divergence analysis.









Below is a further example where we have added one more sample to each group.

title: Inter-media exercise
text:
Now to carry out inter-media divergence analysis.
For this exercise you will create your own code. Solutions are available in the solution boxes below but please make a strong attempt before looking at them.
I would recommend copying, pasting, and editing your code from the inter-site analysis. Ensure you change all the variable names you need to, it is very easy to miss variables and column/row names you need to change.





The steps to carry out this exercise are below along with the solution expandable boxes.


The first step is to create a tibble containing only observations/rows of intra-media distances from the beta_long_tbl tibble. Call this variable: inter_media_wunifrac_long_tbl
Tip: You will need to use the columns media_L and media_R.


Inter-media tibble creation


#Subset long tibble so only rows where media_R and media_L are not identical
#I.e. the long tibble only contains paired distances between samples of 
# different media (inter-media distances)
inter_media_wunifrac_long_tbl <-
    beta_long_tbl |>
        dplyr::filter(media_L != media_R)
#Check head of long df
inter_media_wunifrac_long_tbl |> head()





With the formatted tibble the next step is to create a violin plot. Ensure the x axis is separated by the four media groupings (CVP, ENV, KBC, and TSA). Additionally, colour the points by the paired/right media.
You are aiming for the below plot :
Note: the points are randomly distributed on the x-axis every time you run the command. Therefore yours will most likely look slightly different.





Inter-media violin plot code solution


#Inter-media divergence violin plot
inter_media_violin_plot <-
    inter_site_wunifrac_long_tbl |>
    ggplot2::ggplot(aes(x = media_L, y = value)) +
    ggplot2::geom_violin() +
    ggforce::geom_sina(aes(colour = media_R), alpha=0.5) +
    ggplot2::labs(x = "Media", y = "Weighted UniFrac",
                    title="Inter-media divergence with Weighted UniFrac dissimilarity",
                    subtitle="Points coloured by media of paired distance sample",
                    colour = "Media")
#Save ggplot2 object with ggsave
ggsave(filename = "./wunifrac_inter_media_divergence_violinplot.png",
        plot = inter_media_violin_plot,
        device = "png", dpi = 300, units = "mm", height = 100, width = 150)
#Display plot
IRdisplay::display_png(file = "./wunifrac_inter_media_divergence_violinplot.png")


In the plot we can see:

The ENV samples are highly dissimilar to the CVP, KBC, and TSA samples (>0.5 Weighted UniFrac) with similar distances between these three pairings.
The media samples (CVP, KBC, and TSA) are more similar to each other (<05 Weighted UniFrac) compared to the ENV samples.
CVP and KBC are the two most similar media groupings (i.e. smallest dissimilarity distances).




Finally, carry out the pairwise wilcox tests to determine if there are significant difference between the inter-media distances. Carry this out to compare distances between the four media and to compare the media pairwise distances.


Inter-media pairwise wilcox


pairwise.wilcox.test(inter_media_wunifrac_long_tbl$value,
                        inter_media_wunifrac_long_tbl$media_L)


#Create new tibble for media pair statistics
inter_media_pairs_wunifrac_long_tbl <-
        inter_media_wunifrac_long_tbl |>
                #Retain lower triangle rows
                dplyr::filter(triangle == "lower") |>
                #Convert media_L and media_R to character columns
                #These are originally factors which cannot be ordered alphabetically
                dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(media_L,media_R), as.character)) |>
                #Create new media_L_R column
                #Ensure the first alphabetical media (pmin) is the prefix
                #and the second/last alphabetical media (pmax) is the suffix
                dplyr::mutate(media_L_R = 
                        paste0(pmin(media_L,media_R),"_",pmax(media_L,media_R)))

#Wilcox
pairwise.wilcox.test(inter_media_pairs_wunifrac_long_tbl$value,
                        inter_media_pairs_wunifrac_long_tbl$media_L_R)


In this case you’lld see there is a significant difference between the intra-group distances of all the different media types except for CVP compared to KBC and CVP compared to TSA. From the plot we may expect to see no significant difference between the intra-group divergences of KBC and TSA but this is not the case seemingly.
The media pair inter-group divergence stats shows each pairing is significantly different to every other pairing. Some finer points:

The three pairings of ENV to the media seem very similar to each other but still have significant p-values values (<0.05) even if CVP_ENV and ENV_KBC barely reach the threshold (0.047).
The media media pairings have very strong evidence of being different to each other (p-value = < 2e-16).

The KBC and CVP samples are the most similar
The KBC and TSA samples are the second most similar
The CVP and TSA samples are the least dissimilar in terms of the media pairs

title: Upper triangle
text:
Upper triangle



Below is all the code needed to create the long tibble from the upper triangle.
Note: You can copy, paste, and edit your code for the lower triangle section. Ensure you change all the relevant variable names, strings, annotation, and other code that is different.

#One code cell for the upper triangle long tibble

#Create new upper triangle matrix
upper_tri_mat <- beta_df_mean

#Convert lower triangle and the diagonal to NAs
upper_tri_mat[lower.tri(upper_tri_mat, diag = TRUE)] <- NA

#Convert to long data frame of paired distance values
#We will refer to the different samples in a pair as the left an right pair
beta_long_tbl <- 
    upper_tri_mat |>
        #Convert to data frame
        as.data.frame() |>
        #Create column from row names (Sample_l, l = left)
        tibble::rownames_to_column("Sample_L") |>
        #Longify
        #Set names to "Sample_r" column (r = right)
        tidyr::pivot_longer(!Sample_L, names_to="Sample_R", values_to="value") |>
        #Remove rows with an NA
        tidyr::drop_na() |>
        #Create triangle column containing value "lower" for each row
        #REMEMBER To CHANGE THIS VALUE TO "upper" IF COPYING AND PASTING
        dplyr::mutate(triangle="upper")
#Check head of long tibble
beta_long_tbl |> head()

#Extract metadata from original phyloseq object
metadf <- phyloseq::sample_data(pseq)

#Add metadata for the left samples
metadf_L <-
    #Extend metadf to match order of left samples
    metadf[beta_long_tbl$Sample_L,] |>
    #Convert to tibble for tidyverse manipulation
    tibble::as_tibble() |>
    #Remove sample.name row
    dplyr::select(-1)
#Rename columns so they have "_L" as their suffix
colnames(metadf_L) <- paste0(colnames(metadf_L),"_L")
#Add metadata_L to beta_long_tbl
beta_long_tbl <-
    dplyr::bind_cols(beta_long_tbl, metadf_L)

#Add metadata for the right samples
metadf_R <-
    #Extend metadf to match order of right samples
    metadf[beta_long_tbl$Sample_R,] |>
    #Convert to tibble for tidyverse manipulation
    tibble::as_tibble() |>
    #Remove sample.name row
    dplyr::select(-1)
#Rename columns so they have "_R" as their suffix
colnames(metadf_R) <- paste0(colnames(metadf_R),"_R")
#Add metadata_R to beta_long_tbl
beta_long_tbl <-
    dplyr::bind_cols(beta_long_tbl, metadf_R)
#Check head of our long df
beta_long_tbl |> head()

#Assign to a new variable
beta_upper_long_tbl <- beta_long_tbl

#Remove unwanted metadata objects
rm(metadf_L, metadf_R)

#Check head of our long tibble
beta_upper_long_tbl |> head()

title: Divergence data format
text:
We will create violin plots with ggplot2 similar to the plots we created in the Alpha diversity chapter of our R community analysis workshop.
For this we need to create a long tibble. To carry this out we will:

Load in the distance matrix
Create a long tibble from the lower triangle
Create a long tibble from the upper triangle
Bind the tibble

However, before that let’s see an example square distance matrix and long data frame for divergence analysis.


What’s a tibble?

A tibble is a reimagining of the data.frame object. It is part of the tidyverse suite of packages these materials extensively use. For more information please see: Tidyverse Tibble guide






Our initial dissimilarity distance data is in a square distance matrix. An example is below:


   S1 S2 S3
S1  0  2  3
S2  2  0  5
S3  3  5  0


There are three main sections to this distance matrix.





The lower triangle is the bottom left triangle of unique values.
For example (ignore the NAs):


   S1 S2 S3
S1 NA NA NA
S2  2 NA NA
S3  3  5 NA








The upper triangle is the top right triangle of unique values.
For example (ignore the NAs):


   S1 S2 S3
S1 NA  2  3
S2 NA NA  5
S3 NA NA NA








The diagonal represents the distances of each sample to itself. These are always zero.
For example (ignore the NAs):


   S1 S2 S3
S1  0 NA NA
S2 NA  0 NA
S3 NA NA  0









When the above example distance matrix is converted into a long tibble for divergence analysis it will then look like:


# A tibble: 6 × 3
  Sample_L Sample_R Value
  <chr>    <chr>    <dbl>
1 S1       S2           2
2 S1       S3           3
3 S2       S1           2
4 S2       S3           5
5 S3       S1           3
6 S3       S2           5


Some of the features of this long tibble are:

The “Value” column is the distance between the two samples
Each observation/row has a “Sample_L” and “Sample_R” column to represent the 2 samples the distance is between

The “L” and “R” represent Left and Right. Left/Right has no significant meaning and instead was chosen as the Right samples are right to the Left samples in the tibble.

We do not include the 0 values from the diagonal.
Each value is represented twice, i.e. the lower and upper triangle values are included.

The 2 rows containing the duplicated values are different in which sample is the Left sample and which is the right sample.
This is required for creating inter-group divergence (explained later)


As an example of duplicated values the below data frame shows the distance between S1 and S2 twice. Notice that S1 is the Left sample in the first row but it is the Right sample in the other row.


# A tibble: 2 × 3
  Sample_L Sample_R Value
  <chr>    <chr>    <dbl>
1 S1       S2           2
2 S2       S1           2


With theory covered let’s move onto practice.

title: Iteration task
text:
Superlative! Now that you know how to carry out iterative rarefaction I’ll ask you to do it once more for the phyla data.







Create a rarefaction averaged phyla relative abundance as we have done in the previous chapters but with 1,000 rarefaction iterations. For this task use 153478 (one-five-three-four-seven-eight) as the seed when creating your vector of 1,000 rng seeds. Save this vector of rngseeds to a file called “rngseeds_1000.RData”.






Note



The iterative rarefaction step may take a few minutes.


After creating the relative abundance matrix determine how different the values are compared to the non-rarefied relative abundance with a histogram.
What is the range of the differences compared to the non rarefied relative abundance values?

 -0.00015 to 0.00015 -0.0015 to 0.002 -0.004 to 0.005




Please attempt the task yourself before looking at the solution code block in the below expandable boxes.






NoteCreating vector of random seeds






#Number of rarefaction iterations to be carried out
rarefaction_iters <- 1000
#Create rngseed vector
#Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(153478)
#Create the rngseed vector
#Sample 1000 (number of iters) values from the number range 1-100,000
rngseed_vec <- sample(x=1:100000, size = rarefaction_iters, replace = FALSE)
#Save our rngseed vector
save(rngseed_vec, file="rngseeds_1000.RData")
#Reset seed
set.seed(NULL)










NotePhyla aggregation and iterative rarefaction






#Iterative rarefaction to produce an average rarefied abundance table

#Assign rarefaction size
rarefaction_size <- min(microbiome::readcount(pseq_env_phyla))
#Load our rng seed vector
load("rngseeds_1000.RData")

#Initialise where we will store the output
#In this case we create the first iteration
#Carry out first rarefaction
pseq_rarefy <- phyloseq::rarefy_even_depth(pseq_env_phyla,
                                           sample.size = rarefaction_size,
                                           #First random seed as the rng seed
                                           rngseed = rngseed_vec[1],
                                           replace = FALSE,
                                           verbose = FALSE)
rarefy_phyla_df <- as.data.frame(phyloseq::otu_table(pseq_rarefy))

#Loop through the next 999 iterations
#Add the rarefied values to rarefy_phyla_df
for (i in 2:length(rngseed_vec)){
  #Rarefy
  pseq_rarefy <- phyloseq::rarefy_even_depth(pseq_env_phyla,
                                           sample.size = rarefaction_size,
                                           rngseed = rngseed_vec[i],
                                           replace = FALSE,
                                           verbose = FALSE)
  #Add values to rarefy_phyla_df
  rarefy_phyla_df <- 
    rarefy_phyla_df + as.data.frame(phyloseq::otu_table(pseq_rarefy))
}
#Average the values of the summed relabund phyla_table
rarefy_phyla_mean_df <- rarefy_phyla_df / length(rngseed_vec)
#Remove unwanted objects
rm(pseq_rarefy, rarefy_phyla_df)










NoteRelative abundance transformation






#Convert to relative abundance table
rarefy_i1000_relabund_phyla_df <- dplyr::mutate_all(rarefy_phyla_mean_df, prop.table)
#View relative abundances
rarefy_i1000_relabund_phyla_df










NoteHistogram of difference to non rarefied data






#Value difference matrix
iterative_rarefaction_1000_diff <- 
  as.matrix(phyloseq::otu_table(pseq_env_phyla_relabund) - rarefy_i1000_relabund_phyla_df)
iterative_rarefaction_diff
#Histogram
hist(iterative_rarefaction_diff)












Amazing!
With this section you have learnt:

How to create a vector of rngseeds
How to use rng seeds to carry out iterative rarefaction

In you real life analysis you would not use this method to create relative abundance taxonomy bar charts, you would use the non-rarefied relative abundance. However, this has hopefully given you a good idea of how iterative rarefaction works so we can utilise it the next 2 chapters for alpha and beta diversity analysis.
Feel free to save then close and halt your “Iterating_rarefaction.ipynb” notebook.

title: α plot with stats
text:
Rather than having the plot and stats separate, we can add stats onto our plot. This can be carried out with the function stat_compare_means() from the ggpubr package.







To produce pairwise comparisons with ggpubr::stat_compare_means() we need a list of the comparisons we want to carry out.


First we need to create a character vector of the unique metadata categories.

#Create character vector of unique metadata values (media in this case)
uniq_media_values_chr_vec <- basic_alpha_metrics_tbl |>
    #Extract media as a vector
    dplyr::pull(media) |>
    #Convert to character
    as.character() |>
    #Unique values
    unique()
#View vector
uniq_media_values_chr_vec







TipCookbook links for Tidyverse function used above




dplyr::pull()






We can create this with the function combn(), short for combination. We provide it with the above character vector and following parameters:

m =: The number of elements to choose when creating combinations.

We choose 2 so we get all pair combinations

simplify =: Indicates if the result should be simple (TRUE) or not (FALSE)

TRUE returns a simplified array such as a matrix or a data frame
FALSE returns a list. This is what we want as ggpubr::stat_compare_means() requires a list



#List of comparisons
my_comparisons <- combn(uniq_media_values_chr_vec, m = 2, simplify = FALSE)
#Check contents and structure
my_comparisons
str(my_comparisons)










With our list of comparisons we can add ggpubr::stat_compare_means() to our ggplot2 code. This function will both calculate the Wilcoxon tests and add them to the plot.

#Produce ggplot object of violin plot
alpha_violinplot <- ggplot(basic_alpha_metrics_tbl, aes(x = media, y = value)) +
                            ggplot2::geom_violin() +
                            ggforce::geom_sina(alpha=0.5, aes(color=site)) +
                            ggplot2::labs(color = "Site", x = "Media", y = "Value") +
                            ggplot2::facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free") +
                            #Add comparisons
                            ggpubr::stat_compare_means(comparisons = my_comparisons)
#Save ggplot2 object with ggsave()
ggsave(filename = "./Alpha_diversity_rarefy_iters_media_violinplot_pairwise_wilcox.png", 
       plot = alpha_violinplot,
       device = "png", dpi = 300, units = "mm", height = 150, width = 250)
#Display plot
IRdisplay::display_png(file = "./Alpha_diversity_rarefy_iters_media_violinplot_pairwise_wilcox.png")









ggplot orders the x-axis by alphabetical order. This is not normally wanted so we will convert our media column to a factor and order the levels how we want them.


As the environmental samples can be seen as the baseline we will have them first.

#Set order of media
basic_alpha_metrics_tbl$media <- factor(basic_alpha_metrics_tbl$media,
                                            #Set order of levels
                                            levels = c("ENV", "CVP", "KBC", "TSA"))




The stats in our previous plot were also not in a good order so we’ll also reorder them.






Important



The first comparison in the list is the bottom most stat in the plot. I.e. CVP vs ENV is the first element and KBC vs TSA is the last (6th) element.



#Order comparisons
my_ordered_comparisons <- my_comparisons[c(1,2,6,4,3,5)]
my_ordered_comparisons

You’ll notice this can be quite manual. It can be made easier when doing this yourself to roughly reorder, run the below code for your plot, then fix the stats reorder.



With our media categories and comparisons reordered we can create the final plot.

#Produce ggplot object of violin plot
alpha_violinplot <- ggplot(basic_alpha_metrics_tbl, aes(x = media, y = value)) +
                            ggplot2::geom_violin() +
                            ggforce::geom_sina(alpha=0.5, aes(color=site)) +
                            ggplot2::labs(color = "Site", x = "Media", y = "Value") +
                            ggplot2::facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free") +
                            #Add comparisons
                            ggpubr::stat_compare_means(comparisons = my_ordered_comparisons)
#Save ggplot2 object with ggsave()
ggsave(filename = "./Alpha_diversity_rarefy_iters_media_violinplot_pairwise_wilcox.png", 
       plot = alpha_violinplot,
       device = "png", dpi = 300, units = "mm", height = 150, width = 250)
#Display plot
IRdisplay::display_png(file = "./Alpha_diversity_rarefy_iters_media_violinplot_pairwise_wilcox.png")

title: β considerations
text:
There are many considerations to take in mind when carrying out beta diversity analysis.







There are many beta diversity distances that you can use. Ultimately the choice is yours but our recommendations would be:

Weighted and unweighted unifrac distances if you have a phylogenetic tree
Bray-Curtis and Jaccard distances if you do not have a phylogenetic tree

These 2 sets of distances are very popular and commonly used as the default choices.
There are two distances in each set as one is based on:

Richness (presence/absence): Unweighted unifrac & Jaccard
Richness and abundance values: Weighted unifrac & Bray-Curtis

Normally the measure using abundance values will be more informative. However, it is good to attempt the richness only approach too as it may show something hidden by the inclusion of the abundance data.








A common question is “Which ordination method should I use?” There are many ordination methods with NMDS and PCoA being popular for ordination distance based values (dissimilarity matrices).
Many people choose based on which method is the most informative. They choose the one that shows the best picture and that explains the data the best.
In this case the PCoA plot looks better than the NMDS plot as the PCoA plot has a high % variance explained and it shows more separation of the samples.
If the PCoA plot had a low % variance explained it may be better to choose the NMDS plot. NMDS attempts to explain the data in the number of dimensions chosen by the user. We chose 2 as we want to plot the data in 2 dimensions.
There is one paper that recommends you create, publish, and stick to a statistical plan before carrying out your analysis. The proposal and reasoning is in the following paper: The Power of Microbiome Studies: Some Considerations on Which Alpha and Beta Metrics to Use and How to Report Results








Your data may be very complex and two dimensions may not be sufficient to plot the data. There are two main ways to plot multiple dimensions.


Create multiple 2D plots to compare pairs of axes. If you wanted to plot the first three axes this way you would produce the following scatter plots:

Axis 1 against Axis 2
Axis 1 against Axis 3
Axis 2 against Axis 3

You can use this method to easily visualise as many axes as possible. The drawback is that you can only directly compare two axes in each plot.



You can create an interactive 3D scatter plot with the package plotly using the plot_ly() function (guide).
This allows you to directly compare 3 axes at once. It is interactive, allowing you to change the perspective of the plot. This allows you to choose the best angle to save the image to use in publication. However, you would generally not use this method to compare more than 3 axes.
